title: Correlation Isn't Causation. So What?
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: The author confronts the most common rebuttal to their anti-classroom-technology research, 'that's correlation, not causation,' by pointing out that while not all correlations are causal, all causal effects are correlational, meaning correlation is exactly what one would expect to see if a real causal relationship existed. They lay out a three-step method for moving from correlation toward defensible causal inference: triangulated correlation (checking whether a pattern persists across many independent datasets, unlike the seasonal ice-cream-and-swimming correlation, which vanishes outside summer), converging evidence (whether smaller controlled experiments reproduce the same pattern seen in large assessments), and mechanistic explanation (whether a plausible biological mechanism, like attention or embodied cognition, explains the data better than rival explanations). Applying this framework, they argue classroom technology's negative association with learning uniquely persists across nearly every tested context (PISA, TIMSS, PIRLS, NAEP, ICILS) with no comparably robust positive signal, making the correlation-causation objection a starting point for scrutiny rather than a rebuttal that ends the conversation.
points: The core logical reframe: 'not all correlations are causal – but all causal effects are correlational,' meaning dismissing correlational evidence outright is scientifically and logically misguided, not merely incomplete.

The three-step causal-inference framework (triangulated correlation, converging evidence, mechanistic explanation) gives readers a replicable method for evaluating any 'correlation isn't causation' objection rather than accepting or dismissing it reflexively.

The ice-cream-and-swimming example illustrates a correlation that fails triangulation because it disappears outside summer months and in contexts like indoor pools or year-round swimmers, contrasted with classroom technology's negative association, which persists across PISA, TIMSS, PIRLS, NAEP, and ICILS.

The author notes a specific asymmetry in the evidence: there is no correlation of comparable strength, scale, or reliability suggesting digital technologies systematically improve learning, even as isolated positive findings exist.
quotes: Not all Christians are Catholics – but all Catholics are Christian.
While it's true that no correlation can prove a causal relationship, the problem is that a correlation is exactly the type of relationship we'd expect to see if a causal relationship were present.

Routine digital exposure in instructional settings is associated with weaker academic outcomes in a dose–response pattern across tests (PISA, TIMSS, PIRLS, NAEP, ICILS), states, countries, grade levels, subjects, years, and varied educational systems.
Notably, there is no similarly robust and consistently replicated signal suggesting that digital technologies systematically improve learning.

Data can tell us that a tool is not working, but only mechanism can tell us why. And when a proposed mechanism explains the data better than competing explanations, we are justified in drawing causal inferences.
So yes: correlation isn't causation. But that argument should be seen as the beginning of the conversation – not used to end it.
